title: Cicero and His Friend Atticus
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero spent his life in the thick of Roman politics: consul, orator, exile, and in the end an enemy of Mark Antony. His closest friend, Titus Pomponius Atticus, chose the opposite path. A wealthy knight, Atticus lived in Athens for about twenty years to avoid Rome's civil strife, refused all public office, and kept friendly relations with men on every side.

He was the one person Cicero told everything. More than four hundred of Cicero's letters to Atticus survive, written from 68 to 44 BC. In them Cicero confesses doubts, vanity, fear and grief he showed to no one else. Atticus managed Cicero's money, had copyists produce and circulate his books, looked after his family, sent him help during his exile in 58 BC, and stood by him when his beloved daughter Tullia died in 45 BC.

Atticus's own replies are lost, but Cicero's side shows how much he leaned on him. When Antony's men killed Cicero in 43 BC, Atticus survived the purges, because over the years he had helped people in every faction, including Antony's family. His friend Cornelius Nepos wrote his biography.
lesson: A friend who stays outside your battles can be your steadiest support. Value the person you can tell everything to, and be that person for someone else.
people: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Titus Pomponius Atticus
source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus; Cornelius Nepos, Life of Atticus
